claims.text: Replacing a conventional EAM reference with an ML interatomic potential trained on ab initio liquid configurations will better capture diverse atomic environments in multicomponent HEAs near melting.
The ML reference will improve reference–target phase-space overlap during thermodynamic integration.
The proposed method is applicable to both solid and liquid multicomponent HEAs near their melting temperatures, including equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and refractory HEAs.
Gaussian approximation potentials or moment tensor potentials can serve as thermodynamic-integration references after training on a wide range of ab initio liquid configurations.
At or above approximately 0.9 times the melting temperature, the liquid exhibits a vast array of atomic configurations.
The method is applicable to HEAs containing at least five elements.
The complex chemical landscapes of multicomponent HEAs result in poor representability by conventional EAM methods.
An ML potential can capture many-body interactions and fine variations in local atomic environments.
Capturing many-body interactions and local-environment variations produces a more faithful representation of the liquid configurational space.
EAM models have a fixed functional form that may omit crucial many-body effects.
An ML potential trained on ab initio data can represent a broad spectrum of atomic configurations.
Broader configurational representability improves overlap between the reference and ab initio target phase spaces.
Improved phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration path mismatch and yields more accurate free energies.
The ML reference will reduce integration-path mismatch error by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The ML reference will improve liquid-state structural correlation metrics, indicating better phase-space overlap.
Standard TOR-TILD uses EAM reference potentials that exhibit significant mismatch because they cannot capture the many configurations of the ab initio liquid.
Benefits from the ML reference will be less pronounced in binary or ternary alloys and at temperatures far below melting.
The quantitative mismatch reduction depends on the quality and transferability of the training data and on the ML architecture.
